rules.title: AB 325 (Cartwright Act): ban on use or distribution of common pricing algorithms in restraint of trade
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade. It is also unlawful to use or distribute one while coercing another person to set or adopt a price or commercial term the algorithm recommends for the same or similar products or services in California. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including software, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. Commercial terms include level of service, availability, and output. Distribution includes selling, licensing, or providing access, including by subscription. The end consumer is not a covered person. A companion section (B&P § 16756.1) relaxes pleading: a Cartwright Act complaint only needs plausible factual allegations of a conspiracy and need not exclude the possibility of independent action. The rule applies to all products and services, including rental housing pricing.
rules.key_value: Ban on using/distributing a common pricing algorithm (uses competitor data, used by 2+ persons) as part of a conspiracy, or while coercing adoption of its recommended price/terms
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person using or distributing such an algorithm in California; not limited by building size or age.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to the end consumer of a product or service (excluded from the definition of 'person').
rules.interaction: Does not impair or limit the applicability of other antitrust laws (B&P Code § 16729(c)).
rules.citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729 (AB 325, Stats. 2025, ch. 338)
rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

rules.title: California application screening fee cap and screening-fee procedures (Civil Code 1950.6)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may charge a residential rental applicant an application screening fee of no more than the actual out-of-pocket cost of gathering information about the applicant, and in no case more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually by CPI beginning January 1, 1998). No fee may be charged when the landlord knows or should know no unit is or will soon be available. A fee may be charged only if the landlord offers either (A) a first-come process: completed applications considered in order received, written screening criteria provided with the application, the first qualifying applicant approved, and no fee charged unless the application is actually considered (fees inadvertently collected from concurrent submissions must be refunded within 7 days or, at the applicant's option, applied to another unit), or (B) a full refund to every applicant not selected, within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of submission, whichever is first. The landlord must give an itemized receipt (personally, by mail, or by agreed email), return any unused portion if no reference check or credit report is obtained, and give the applicant a copy of the credit report within 7 days of receiving it. Landlords may accept reusable screening reports under Section 1950.1. The fee is not security under Section 1950.5.

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act – just cause for termination of tenancy
rules.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the unit for 12 months (or, if adult tenants were added before 24 months, all tenants for 12 months or one tenant for 24 months), the owner may not terminate the tenancy without an at-fault or no-fault just cause, which must be stated in the written termination notice. Curable lease violations require a notice and opportunity to cure first. For no-fault terminations (owner/relative move-in, withdrawal from rental market, government order, demolition or substantial remodel), the owner must either pay relocation assistance equal to one month's rent within 15 calendar days of service of the notice or waive the final month's rent, and must tell the tenant of this right in the notice. Owner move-in requires that the intended occupant move in within 90 days and live there 12 months, or the unit must be re-offered at the same rent with reimbursement of moving expenses. Substantial remodel notices must include specified statements, a description of the work and permits. Owners must give tenants a specified notice of these protections in at least 12-point type. Waivers are void.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 12 months of occupancy; no-fault terminations require relocation assistance or rent waiver equal to one month's rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property where the tenant has occupied 12+ months; excludes housing with a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years and property covered by a local just cause ordinance (pre-9/1/2019, or later and more protective).
rules.exemptions: Transient/tourist hotels; nonprofit hospitals, religious, extended care, licensed elder/adult residential facilities; school/university dormitories; units where tenant shares bath or kitchen with resident owner; single-family owner-occupied residences renting no more than two units or bedrooms (including ADU/JADU) and mobilehomes; owner-occupied duplex (owner occupied one unit at start of tenancy and continues); housing with certificate of occupancy within previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome); separately alienable units (e.g., single-family homes, condos) not owned by a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, if tenants received the statutory exemption notice; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; homeowners of mobilehomes; property subject to a qualifying local just cause ordinance.
rules.interaction: Does not apply where a local just cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019 applies, or where a later-adopted or amended local ordinance is more protective (with a binding local finding), in which case the local ordinance applies. A property cannot be subject to both. Local ordinances adopted after September 1, 2019 that are less protective may not be enforced unless this section is repealed. Relocation assistance under this section is credited against relocation required by other law. rules.title: California FEHA housing discrimination: source-of-income protection and credit-history alternatives for subsidized applicants
rules.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against applicants or tenants based on source of income. Source of income means lawful, verifiable income, including public assistance and housing subsidies such as Section 8 vouchers and HUD-VASH vouchers. Owners may not publish ads stating a source-of-income preference or limitation. Income standards must count the combined income of people who will live together, on the same basis as married couples. Where there is a government rent subsidy, owners must apply income standards only to the tenant's share of the rent. They also may not use credit history unless they offer the applicant the option of providing alternative evidence of ability to pay that share, such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements. Owners may still ask about the level or source of income, verify employment, request landlord references, and verify identity.

rules.title: California security deposit limits and return rules (Civil Code 1950.5)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security, however labeled, of more than one month's rent on top of first month's rent. A small landlord may charge up to two months' rent if it is a natural person, or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, and owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than 4 units in total. That exception does not apply to service member tenants. An advance payment of at least six months' rent is allowed on leases of six months or longer. Since April 1, 2025, a higher deposit charged to a service member must be explained in writing and returned after 6 months without rent arrears. Deductions are limited to unpaid rent, tenant-caused damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning to move-in condition, and restoring personal property. The tenant may request an initial pre-move-out inspection and must receive an itemized statement of proposed deductions. Landlords must photograph the unit at move-in (tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025), after move-out, and after repairs. Within 21 calendar days after move-out, the landlord must give an itemized statement with receipts and invoices and return the balance, electronically if the deposit or rent was paid electronically. rules.title: Massachusetts security deposit law
rules.requirement: A security deposit may not exceed one month's rent. It must be held in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, beyond the reach of the lessor's creditors. rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: Makes it unlawful under the New Jersey Antitrust Act for a rental property owner (or its agent) to pay for or use the services of a coordinator. Coordinators may not facilitate anticompetitive agreements, and no person may engage in parallel pricing coordination or perform a coordinating function. Exclusions cover research, free public rent estimates, equal-access brokerage listing databases that do not set or recommend prices, and government affordability controls. The Attorney General must set up a complaint portal and may adopt rules.

rules.title: Jersey City Rent Control Ordinance (Chapter 260)
rules.requirement: Rent on covered units is regulated under the Jersey City Rent Control Ordinance, administered and enforced by the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations. Properties with 1-4 units are exempt. Increases beyond the ordinary limit require landlord applications (capital improvement, vacancy capital improvement, hardship). Tenants may file Illegal Rent Petitions or Failure to Maintain Service Petitions for rent reductions.
rules.key_value: Rent control applies to properties with 5 or more units. The page references a CPI chart but does not state the allowable annual increase.
rules.coverage_conditions: Properties with 5 or more units, unless an exemption is granted under the ordinance.
rules.exemptions: All 1-4 unit properties are exempt. The ordinance provides other exemptions, available through a Rent Control Exemption Request; the criteria are not listed on this page.
rules.quoted_span: (Please Note: All 1-4 Unit Properties are exempt from rent control)

no_rule_findings.finding: State law bars Massachusetts cities and towns from enacting, maintaining or enforcing rent control of any kind. The only exception is a narrow voluntary, municipally compensated regime under chapter 40P.
no_rule_findings.quoted_span: No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind

no_rule_findings.finding: Under G.L. c.186 § 12, a tenancy at will in Massachusetts may be ended by either party with written notice, and the statute lists no required grounds. At the state level it therefore permits termination without cause; it sets only notice periods and a nonpayment cure right. This section creates no state just-cause rule. Local ordinances are not addressed in this document.
no_rule_findings.quoted_span: Estates at will may be determined by either party by three months' notice in writing for that purpose given to the other party

no_rule_findings.finding: The article indicates Massachusetts currently has no rent control: the ballot question sought to bring it back, and that question was struck from the 2026 ballot.
